subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the Eduqas spec.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for GCSE Eduqas Biology simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake.

questions.q: What is the correct pathway of a nervous response to a stimulus?
options: stimulus -> receptor -> sensory neurone -> CNS -> motor neurone -> effector
questions.explain: The pathway is: stimulus -> receptor -> sensory neurone -> CNS (coordinator) -> motor neurone -> effector (muscle or gland) -> response.

questions.q: The central nervous system (CNS) consists of the:
questions.explain: The CNS is made up of the brain and spinal cord. It coordinates the response, receiving information from receptors and sending instructions to effectors.

questions.q: At a synapse, how is the signal transmitted between two neurones?
options: By an electrical spark jumping the gap
By a chemical neurotransmitter diffusing across the gap
questions.explain: At a synapse the electrical impulse triggers release of a chemical neurotransmitter, which diffuses across the gap and binds to receptors on the next neurone, continuing the impulse.

questions.q: Why are reflex actions important?
options: They are rapid and automatic, protecting the body from harm
questions.explain: Reflex actions are rapid and automatic and do not involve conscious thought, protecting the body (e.g. pulling a hand from a hot object). The impulse passes through a reflex arc.

questions.q: In a reflex arc, which neurone connects the sensory neurone to the motor neurone in the spinal cord?
questions.explain: In a reflex arc a relay neurone (interneurone) in the CNS connects the sensory neurone to the motor neurone, bypassing conscious brain processing for speed.

questions.q: Which part of the eye contains the light receptor cells?
questions.explain: The retina at the back of the eye contains light receptor cells (rods and cones). The cornea and lens focus light; the iris controls pupil size.

questions.q: In bright light, the iris muscles adjust the pupil so that it:
options: Gets larger to let in more light
Gets smaller to let in less light and protect the retina
questions.explain: In bright light the circular muscles of the iris contract and radial muscles relax, making the pupil smaller to reduce light entering and protect the retina.

questions.q: To focus on a NEAR object, the ciliary muscles contract and the lens becomes:
questions.explain: For near objects the ciliary muscles contract, suspensory ligaments slacken, and the lens becomes thicker and more curved (accommodation) to refract light more strongly.

questions.q: Which part of the brain controls balance and coordination of muscular activity?
questions.explain: The cerebellum controls balance and fine coordination of movement. The cerebral cortex handles consciousness and memory; the medulla controls unconscious activities like heart rate.

questions.q: How do hormones travel around the body?
questions.explain: Hormones are chemical messengers made by endocrine glands and carried dissolved in the blood plasma to target organs. Hormonal responses are slower but longer-lasting than nervous ones.

questions.q: Adrenaline, released from the adrenal glands, prepares the body for:
options: 'Fight or flight' by increasing heart rate and blood glucose
questions.explain: Adrenaline is released in frightening/stressful situations, increasing heart rate, breathing rate and blood glucose to prepare the body for 'fight or flight'.

questions.q: (Higher tier) Thyroxine controls the basal metabolic rate and is regulated by:
options: Positive feedback that keeps increasing it
Negative feedback that keeps its level steady
questions.explain: Thyroxine, from the thyroid gland, sets the basal metabolic rate. Its level is controlled by negative feedback: high thyroxine reduces its own further release, keeping levels stable.

questions.q: Which hormone is released when blood glucose concentration is too HIGH?
questions.explain: When blood glucose is too high, the pancreas releases insulin, which causes cells (especially liver and muscle) to take up glucose and store it as glycogen, lowering blood glucose.

questions.q: In Type 1 diabetes the pancreas does not produce enough insulin. It is usually treated by:
questions.explain: Type 1 diabetes is treated with insulin injections and careful diet/exercise to control blood glucose. Type 2 is often managed by diet and exercise as cells stop responding to insulin.

questions.q: Homeostasis is best defined as:
options: Maintaining a stable internal environment despite external changes
The loss of water from leaves
The movement of water into cells
questions.explain: Homeostasis is the regulation of the internal conditions of the body (e.g. temperature, blood glucose, water) to maintain a stable internal environment for cells to function.

questions.q: When the body is too hot, one response is:
options: Sweating and vasodilation to lose heat
questions.explain: When too hot, sweat glands release more sweat (evaporation cools the skin) and skin blood vessels vasodilate so more blood flows near the surface, radiating heat away.

questions.q: (Separate science) What is the main role of the kidneys?
options: Filtering the blood to remove urea and adjust water and salt balance
questions.explain: The kidneys filter the blood, removing urea (a waste product of protein breakdown) and excess water and salts, producing urine while reabsorbing useful substances like glucose.

questions.q: (Separate science, Higher) When the body is dehydrated, the hormone ADH causes the kidneys to:
options: Reabsorb more water, producing less concentrated urine
Reabsorb more water, producing a smaller volume of more concentrated urine
questions.explain: When dehydrated, more ADH is released, making the kidney tubules more permeable so more water is reabsorbed. This produces a small volume of concentrated urine (negative feedback).

questions.q: A plant shoot growing towards light is showing:
questions.explain: Growth towards light is positive phototropism, controlled by the hormone auxin. Shoots grow towards light to maximise photosynthesis; roots show positive gravitropism (geotropism).

questions.q: Auxin causes a shoot to bend towards light because it:
options: Accumulates on the shaded side, causing faster growth so the shoot bends towards the light
Accumulates on the lighter side, slowing growth there
Is destroyed by light everywhere equally
questions.explain: Auxin accumulates on the shaded side of the shoot, where it stimulates cell elongation. That side grows faster, so the shoot bends towards the light (positive phototropism).
